Jean d'Estrées was a French priest and politician, born on 1666 in Paris, who played a significant role in the governance of Western Europe during the Early Modern period. He was the son of Jean II d'Estrées and his wife Marie Marguerite Morin, and succeeded his father as a prominent figure in French politics. Jean d'Estrées served as a diplomat and advisor to the French government, and his influence extended to the royal court and the French Parliament. He was also a key figure in the development of the French Enlightenment, advocating for the principles of reason and tolerance. Through his work, Jean d'Estrées helped shape the course of French history, leaving a lasting legacy in the realms of politics, philosophy, and culture. His contributions to the French Enlightenment can be seen in the writings of prominent thinkers such as Voltaire and Rousseau, who were influenced by his ideas on liberty and democracy.

As a priest, Jean d'Estrées was deeply committed to the spiritual and moral values of the Catholic Church, and he worked tirelessly to promote the teachings of the Church throughout his life. His dedication to the Church's mission was evident in his efforts to establish new parishes and schools, and to promote the spiritual well-being of the faithful. Despite his many accomplishments, Jean d'Estrées remains a relatively unknown figure in the annals of history, overshadowed by more prominent figures of the time. Nevertheless, his contributions to French politics, philosophy, and culture make him an important figure to be remembered and studied.
